messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thomas Jensen was thirty‑seven when the storm hit. A quiet night in the small coastal town where he served as a military medic, a freak squall turned the highway into a torrent of wind‑blasted debris and the sea into a churned wall. He was on duty, triaging a collapsed bridge crew, when the sky opened and a sudden, violent roar of the storm tore through the air, sending a jagged lightning bolt right over the field. The blast of thunder and the hiss of the wind felt like a barrage aimed directly at his ears. He dropped the first aid kit he was holding and ran to cover the wounded soldiers, all the while hearing the relentless pounding of the storm and the frantic shouts of his teammates. The night ended with a single, blood‑tinged memory of the flash of lightning striking a nearby tree, splitting it in two, and the terrified screams of the injured. The rawness of that image has never faded. When Thomas tries to talk about the night, he finds himself slipping into a maze of images. He can recall the roar of the thunder, the flash of the lightning, the splintered tree, but the sequence feels scrambled. “I know one thing, that it was a storm, but the rest is like a dream I can’t put in order,” he says. The terror that floods him when he recalls the event feels exactly the same as the instant he witnessed the tree shatter. He reaches for his first aid kit again in his mind, feels the weight of it, and suddenly is overwhelmed by emotions so strong that he must stop, his chest tightening, his thoughts racing. What he fears most is that remembering the scene might bring back the same terror and that would make him feel like he’s back in the storm, again and again. Because he has lost faith in the safety that the world should offer, he now believes that the very act of remembering will resurrect the chaos. His identity as a calm, dependable medic has been shaken, and he feels that no part of himself is secure. Thomas’s heightened sense of threat has seeped into every corner of his life. He cannot relax, not even when he is alone in his apartment. A sudden, loud noise—a car back‑firing or a door slamming—sets him on high alert. He keeps his eyes peeled for signs of danger, feeling the pulse of fear under his skin. He is convinced that the world has turned into a hostile place where anything can happen at any moment. Because of this constant hypervigilance, he no longer feels that his sense of order and control matters. He has begun to view the world as a place where the unexpected is inevitable, which further erodes his sense of meaning and strengthens the belief that he has lost himself. The fear that a sudden sound might signal another catastrophe pushes him to avoid many aspects of his previous routine, including the field work he once enjoyed. At the base, where Thomas used to perform routine triage during training drills, the echoes of thunder and the sharp clangs of equipment now feel like reminders of that night. He has begun to skip the drills, preferring to stay in the infirmary and stay near the first aid supplies, thinking that being in a “safe place” will keep him protected. The avoidance has taken a toll on his career. A senior medic recently pointed out that Thomas's absence from drills has compromised team readiness, and his superiors have started to question his reliability. Thomas feels a new, crushing weight of guilt—his own avoidance has caused a ripple of distress for his colleagues. He cannot shake the sense that the world’s meaning has dissolved, and that he has no identity beyond the trauma. Now, months after the storm, Thomas sits in a therapist’s office, eyes flicking to the window and back to the clinician’s notebook. He is here because he can no longer manage the constant fear of sudden sounds, and because the terror that erupts whenever he remembers the night keeps him from sleeping, from feeling secure, and from performing his duties. What he fears most is that the cycle will keep tightening until he can no longer function, but he also hopes that, with help, he can reclaim the calm he once felt in the quiet moments between patrols.
